question.:question/problem: Find the derivative of $y = \cot (\cos x)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\cot{\left(u \right)},\qquad u=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=- \cot^{2}{\left(u \right)} - 1,\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \sin{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ &=(- \cot^{2}{\left(u \right)} - 1)\cdot (- \sin{\left(x \right)}) \\ &=- \left(- \cot^{2}{\left(\cos{\left(x \right)} \right)} - 1\right) \sin{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =\cos \left(\sin x \right)$ at the point $\left(0,1 \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = \cos{u}, \qquad u = \sin x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = -\sin{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=-\sin u \cdot (\cos x)\\
&=-\cos x \sin (\sin x).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(0)&=-\cos (0) \sin (\sin (0))\\
	&=-1 \cdot 0 \\
        &=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,1) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-1 &= (0)\cdot\left(x-0\right)\\
y&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =\cos{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}$ at the point $\left(0,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{6}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)})\\
&=- \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(0)&=- \sin{\left(\sin{\left(0 \right)} + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\
        &=- \frac{1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) &= (- \frac{1}{2})\cdot\left(x-(0)\right)\\
y&=- \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =5 \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)}$ at the point $\left(0,0 \right).$

$y=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = 5 \cos{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u = \sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = - 5 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\
&=- 5 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)})\\
&=- 5 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find
$$
\begin{aligned}
	f'(0)&=- 5 \sin{\left(\sin{\left(0 \right)} + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)} \cos{\left(0 \right)}\\
	&=-5 \cdot 1 \\
        &=-5.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,0) \mathbin{:}$


$$
\begin{aligned}
y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\
y-\left(0\right) &= (-5)\cdot\left(x-(0)\right)\\
y&=- 5 x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $y=7\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)),$ we have

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡($
{{field-2}} $).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=7\operatorname{cos}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\  & =-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)),$ we have

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \,\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡($
{{field-2}} $).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡(x).

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $y=8\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)),$ we have

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \,\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡($
{{field-2}} $).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =8\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =-8\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the derivative of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\csc^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-\csc^{2}⁡u\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\csc^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the derivative of $y=\sin{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\sin{\left(u \right)},\qquad u=\sin{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\cos{\left(u \right)},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ &=(\cos{\left(u \right)})\cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &=\cos{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$
